title: How to film a reference video for AI motion transfer
summary: Film a usable AI motion-transfer reference. Set the frame for footwork, hand gestures and turns, then test the difficult part before animating.
body_markdown:
Film one continuous take with one visible performer, a steady camera, and enough room to see the joints and contact points that matter. Frame a dance wide enough to keep the feet in the shot. Frame a gesture close enough to see the hands. The reference clip supplies the performance, so make that performance clear before you spend credits animating it.


## Set the frame for the movement you need


Decide what the viewer must recognize. For a dance, watch the feet land and keep the whole turn in frame. For a product gesture, keep the hands, the object and the point of contact visible. If the character only needs to nod or react, a closer frame gives the head and shoulders more of the image.


Hold the camera still for the first take. Give the performer room at both edges and check the frame at the widest reach of the move. Use even light and enough contrast for the limbs to stand out from the background. Record a moment of the starting and ending pose, then trim the reference to the move you want to transfer. If the plan is to cut from a wide shot to a close-up, film and process those references separately.


## Pair the reference with a character image that can perform it


Choose an image that shows the parts of the character you need to move. For a full-body step, start with a full-body image and room for the character to travel in the frame. For a seated hand gesture, check that the image has the framing you want and that important objects are visible. If a wide move keeps failing with a tight portrait, try an image with a wider composition before recutting the motion.


[Magic Hour Motion Control](https://magichour.ai/products/motion-control) uses a motion-reference video and a character image. In Animate, the image supplies the scene as well as the character. If the original video’s background and camera framing are part of what must stay, use the[Character Replace workflow](https://magichour.ai/blog/how-to-replace-a-character-in-a-video-with-ai-for-free) .


## Test the hardest part of the take


Try the short section with the turn, fast step or object contact that has to work. Keep the same character image while comparing two reference takes so you can see whether the movement or the framing caused the difference.


**What you need to see**


**What to check in the source take**


A turn that reads clearly


The performer stays in frame through the back-facing portion and return.


Footwork that lands on a beat


Both feet remain visible near the edge of the frame and on each landing.


A hand reaches a prop


The wrist, fingers and contact point stay visible during the reach.


A repeatable loop


The final pose and framing can cut back to the opening without a jump you need to hide.


Review the finished clip at normal speed first. If it loses the motion in one spot, return to the matching timestamp in the reference. A cropped hand calls for reframing. A busy background or another person passing in front calls for a cleaner take. If the output needs to match a beat, check the final motion against the track in your editor before processing the rest.


## Watch where the image and motion go


[Watch the walkthrough on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eS3dqwxowvY) .


Magic Hour’s tutorial shows the Animate and Replace inputs. The shooting checklist above is for preparing your own reference, so use footage you own or have permission to reuse. For a broader choice of tools, see the[motion control comparison](https://magichour.ai/blog/best-ai-motion-control-tools) .
